subject: biology
title: Base Pairs & Population Data
welcome_lead: Today you'll crack the DNA code — the rules that pair the bases A-T and C-G — and read data tables showing how traits vary in real populations.
meta_desc: GCSE Biology DNA base pairing — complementary strands (A-T, C-G), interpreting variation data tables.
final_note: You learned that A pairs with T, C pairs with G, how to write a complementary strand, and how to read variation data from a population.

walkthroughs.body_html:
DNA has only 4 letters: A, T, C, G.

They're called bases. Their order spells the genetic message.

The two strands hold hands using strict rules:

A always pairs with T · C always pairs with G.

So if one strand reads A-T-C-G, the other must read T-A-G-C. Easy!

Surveys count traits in real populations — eye colour, height, blood group.

Look for the most common trait and the spread. Continuous traits (height) form a curve; discrete traits (blood group) form bars.

mcqs.q: What does it mean for an allele to be 'dominant'?
options: It is expressed in the phenotype when at least one copy is present (in a heterozygote).
A dominant allele physically destroys the recessive allele in the genome.
Humans evolved from monkeys but chimps evolved from gorillas.
A dominant allele is the most common allele in a population.

mcqs.q: How does a population of organisms become better adapted to its environment over time?
options: A dominant allele physically destroys the recessive allele in the genome.
Organisms decide what features they need and grow them by force of will.
Individuals with advantageous heritable variations survive and reproduce more; their alleles increase in frequency over generations.
Individual organisms change during their lifetime in response to their environment and pass the changes on to offspring.
Humans evolved directly from chimpanzees, which is why chimps still exist as a less-evolved version.
No — humans and chimpanzees share a common ancestor; both have evolved from it.
